title: Deadlock: Two Transactions, Opposite Lock Order
description: Two transactions updating rows in opposite order deadlock; access rows in a consistent order to break the cycle. Why it matters: deadlocks are a top cause of mysterious, intermittent transaction failures in production -- and consistent access ordering is the single cheapest way to prevent them.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About

Picture two cars arriving at a single-lane bridge from opposite ends at exactly the same moment. Each one has already driven halfway across before noticing the other. Neither can go forward without hitting the other car, and neither can back up without giving way first — so if neither driver yields, they simply sit there forever. That gridlock is a deadlock, and this lesson is about the database version of exactly that situation.

**What this lesson's topic actually is.** A deadlock happens when two separate transactions (again, think of a transaction as "a bundle of changes that either all succeed together or all fail together") each hold onto something the other one needs, and each is waiting for the other to let go first. Since both are waiting, and neither will ever let go until it gets what it's waiting for, they're stuck in a permanent standoff. SQL Server is smart enough to notice this and doesn't just let both sessions hang forever — it forcibly kills one of them (calls it the "deadlock victim") with an error, so the other one can proceed.

**Why this happens in real databases.** This lesson is specifically about the classic cause: two transactions that update the same two rows, but in the opposite order from each other. Say Transaction 1 needs to update Row X first, then Row Y. Transaction 2, running at the same time, needs to update Row Y first, then Row X. If they interleave just wrong — Transaction 1 grabs Row X, Transaction 2 grabs Row Y, at almost the exact same instant — then each transaction is now holding one of the two rows the other one needs next, and each is blocked waiting for the other's row. This is extremely common in real applications precisely because it doesn't require any single piece of code to be "wrong" — it happens purely because of unlucky timing between two pieces of code that are each individually perfectly reasonable. A batch job processing accounts in ID order, and a user-triggered transfer that happens to touch the same two accounts in reverse — that's all it takes.

**How it happens mechanically inside SQL Server.** Remember from the locking lesson that an `UPDATE` takes an exclusive lock on the row it changes, and holds that lock until the whole transaction commits or rolls back. Now walk through the sequence: Transaction 1 runs `UPDATE ... WHERE Id = X`, gets the exclusive lock on row X. At virtually the same moment, Transaction 2 runs `UPDATE ... WHERE Id = Y`, gets the exclusive lock on row Y. So far, no conflict — they own different rows. But then Transaction 1's next statement is `UPDATE ... WHERE Id = Y` — it needs row Y, which Transaction 2 already owns. Transaction 1 blocks, waiting for Transaction 2 to finish and release row Y. Meanwhile, Transaction 2's next statement is `UPDATE ... WHERE Id = X` — it needs row X, which Transaction 1 already owns. Transaction 2 also blocks. Now you have a genuine cycle: 1 is waiting on 2, and 2 is waiting on 1, and neither will ever finish because finishing is exactly what the other one is waiting for.

SQL Server runs a background process (the "deadlock monitor") that periodically checks the chain of who's-waiting-on-whom, looking specifically for these cycles. When it finds one, it has to break the cycle somehow — it can't let both sessions wait forever, since that would eventually stack up more and more blocked work behind them. It picks one of the two transactions as the "victim" (usually the one that's cheaper to undo) and kills it immediately with error 1205, rolling back all of its changes. The other transaction is freed to continue and complete normally.

**Why this matters in production.** Deadlocks are one of the most notorious and hardest-to-reproduce categories of bug in real systems. They are inherently a race condition — they only occur when two specific transactions happen to overlap in time in exactly the wrong way, hitting the same two rows in reverse order within a small window. A developer testing manually, one request at a time, will essentially never trigger one. They show up in production under real concurrent load, often intermittently and unpredictably, and the application sees an error (SqlException, error number 1205) on a transaction that had nothing wrong with it — it was simply the unlucky one selected as the victim. Because the failure looks random and the query that failed looks totally fine in isolation, deadlocks are notoriously confusing to diagnose without knowing this underlying mechanism.

The fix has nothing to do with rewriting a query to be "more efficient" — the two update statements were fine — it's about coordination. If every transaction touching rows X and Y always accesses them in the same order (say, always row X before row Y, regardless of which one the business logic thinks of "first"), then it becomes impossible for two transactions to each be holding one row while waiting on the other, and the cycle can never form in the first place. This lesson lets you watch this exact race happen live, see the deadlock error appear, and then reorder the statements to eliminate it.

**Try it yourself.** The interactive scenario below lets you fire off both transactions and watch SQL Server's deadlock monitor catch the cycle and kill one of the two sessions with error 1205. Notice that neither transaction's individual statements look wrong at all in isolation — the deadlock exists purely because of the order in which the two rows are touched relative to each other. Once you fix the ordering so both transactions always touch the rows in the same sequence, run it again and watch the deadlock disappear entirely, with both transactions completing normally, one simply waiting briefly behind the other instead of both getting stuck in a cycle.

**Beyond this exact scenario.** The opposite-order shape isn't limited to two explicit `UPDATE` statements written by the same developer — it just as easily arises between two entirely different features written by different teams, months apart, that happen to touch the same two tables in reverse order without either team knowing about the other. A nightly batch job processing accounts in ID order and an interactive "transfer funds" feature processing them in whatever order the user picked the accounts on screen is a completely realistic, very common real-world instance of exactly this pattern, and it's worth actively auditing for whenever two pieces of code touch the same set of tables.

## Scenario
A money-transfer routine updates two accounts per transaction. Session A transfers 1→2, Session B transfers 2→1. Under load they intermittently fail with *"Transaction was deadlocked ... chosen as the deadlock victim."*

## Why it happens
A updates row **1** (takes X lock on 1), B updates row **2** (X lock on 2). Now A wants row 2 (held by B) and B wants row 1 (held by A). Each waits for the other — a **cycle**. SQL Server's deadlock monitor detects it and kills the cheaper transaction as the **victim** (error 1205), rolling it back.

## What to look for
- Timeline: A acquires lock on 1, B acquires lock on 2, both then **block** on the other's row, one becomes the **deadlock victim**.
- The deadlock graph shows two processes each holding one resource and requesting the other.

## The concept
Deadlocks from **inconsistent lock ordering** are fixed by imposing a **consistent order**: always touch accounts in ascending `AccountId`. With a global ordering the cycle can't form — the second session just waits briefly, then proceeds. (Keeping transactions short and having the right indexes also reduces the deadlock window.)
startingQuery: -- This is a concurrency lesson. Reorder the statements so both sessions lock rows in the same order, then Run.
hints: Watch the lock order: A locks 1 then 2; B locks 2 then 1. That opposite order is the cycle.
If both sessions always lock the LOWER AccountId first, no cycle can form.
Reorder Session B to update AccountId 1 before AccountId 2 (ascending order in both).

interleaving.description: A locks 1 then wants 2; B locks 2 then wants 1 -> deadlock.

A.sql: BEGIN TRAN; UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance - 100 WHERE AccountId = 1;
UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance + 100 WHERE AccountId = 2; COMMIT;

B.sql: BEGIN TRAN; UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance - 50 WHERE AccountId = 2;
UPDATE Accounts SET Balance = Balance + 50 WHERE AccountId = 1; COMMIT;

interleaving.solutionNote: Make both sessions update AccountId 1 before AccountId 2 (consistent ascending lock order). The cycle cannot form, so no deadlock.
